conceptTag: How a niche brand beats big brands
readerTitle: Why the small glove maker keeps winning the freezer
caseNote: 가상 사례 (냉동 창고용 장갑 제조사, 동물병원 예약 소프트웨어) · 실제 기업이나 수치 없음
insight: 작은 브랜드는 모두에게 조금 더 나은 것이 아니라, 한 집단에게 훨씬 나은 것으로 이긴다. 큰 브랜드는 바로 그 좁힘을 따라 하기 어렵다.
misconception: 큰 브랜드가 더 싼 제품을 내놓으면 작은 브랜드도 가격을 맞추거나 시장을 넓혀야 살아남는다.

sources.text: Porter, M. (1980). Competitive Strategy. Free Press. (집중 전략과 차별화의 개념)

factChecks.note: 냉동 창고 온도 "약 −25°C"는 일반적인 냉동 물류 창고 범위(대략 −18°C~−30°C)를 가정한 설명용 수치입니다. 게시 전 업계 자료로 범위를 확인하세요.
장갑 제조사, 대형 브랜드의 30% 저가 제품, 소매 체인 제안, 동물병원 소프트웨어는 모두 가상 사례입니다. 실제 기업과 겹치지 않는지 확인하세요.
새 개념을 도입하지 않고 STR-03-03(집중)과 STR-03-02(차별화)만 적용했는지, 판단 문제 피드백에 개념 이름이 들어갔는지 확인했습니다.

cards.title: Why the small glove maker keeps winning the freezer
body: 6 a.m. in a freezer warehouse, around −25°C. A picker pulls off a thick glove from a famous brand to tap her scanner screen. Within a minute her fingers sting.
Down the aisle, a coworker scans without stopping. His gloves come from a company most people have never heard of. That small company was built around this exact moment.

image.label: Warehouse worker scanning boxes in a frosty freezer aisle
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 서리 낀 냉동 창고 통로, 두 작업자. 한 명은 두꺼운 장갑을 벗어 들고 손을 호호 불고, 다른 한 명은 얇아 보이는 장갑을 낀 채 바코드 스캐너 화면을 누른다. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: A giant launches a cheaper cold glove.
body: You make gloves for freezer warehouse pickers: touchscreen fingertips, grip on frosty plastic, warm for an eight-hour shift. A big brand launches an insulated glove "for every cold job" at 30% less than yours.

options.feedback: You'd fight on cost, where the giant's volume wins. You give up margin and still look like a smaller version of them.

options.text: Go deeper on pickers: test grip on frozen cartons, sell straight to warehouse safety managers
options.feedback: This is **focus** plus **differentiation**: serve one group so well that a glove made for everyone feels like a compromise to them.

options.text: Add ski, cycling and construction lines to grow volume
options.feedback: More customers, but each new group pulls the design a different way. You risk becoming a weaker copy of the big brand.

cards.title: "Good for everyone" wasn't good enough here.
body: The giant's glove is fine for shoveling snow or loading a truck. But a freezer picker scans hundreds of items a shift and handles frosty shrink-wrap.
The person who buys is the warehouse safety manager. They count dropped items, slow scans and cold-injury reports. For them, a glove that saves a few seconds per pick is worth far more than 30% off.
The small brand lost almost nobody it was built for.

cards.title: Narrow the target, then be different for it.
body: **Focus** means choosing a narrow group and serving it better than broad rivals can. **Differentiation** means being different in ways customers value and will pay for.
Alone, each is weaker. A narrow target with an ordinary product is just a small business. A special feature aimed at everyone gets copied. Together, the niche tells you *which* differences matter.

image.label: Wide spotlight versus a narrow, bright spotlight
image.brief: 두 개의 조명 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽: 넓고 흐린 조명이 다양한 작업자(스키어, 건설 인부, 창고 작업자)를 비춤, 라벨 "Big brand: everyone". 오른쪽: 좁고 밝은 조명이 냉동 창고 작업자 한 명만 비춤, 라벨 "Niche brand: one job". 로고 없음.

cards.title: Its size is the reason it can't narrow down.
body: The giant could make a freezer-picker glove. Here's why it usually doesn't:
list: It sells through big stores that want one product for many buyers
A niche line is too small to matter in its sales targets
Tuning for pickers, like thinner fingertips, would make the glove worse for its other customers
cards.callout: What looks like your weakness, being small and narrow, is what keeps them out.

cards.title: A big retailer wants your gloves, with changes.
body: A national hardware chain offers to stock you in every store, if you make a cheaper version without the touchscreen tips. Meanwhile, meat-packing plants and refrigerated-truck drivers have started asking about your gloves.

options.text: Take the retail deal and make the cheaper version
options.feedback: Big volume, but you remove the very thing that sets you apart. That gives up your **differentiation** and puts you head to head with the giant.

options.text: Sell the same glove to meat plants and cold-chain drivers
options.feedback: These buyers share the job: cold hands doing precise work. You grow while keeping your **focus** and the features they pay for.

options.text: Stay put and raise prices, since pickers are loyal
options.feedback: You may earn more per glove, but you skip nearby customers who need the same thing. Loyalty also has limits.

cards.title: A niche only works under two conditions.
body: First, the group must be big enough and willing to pay more. A perfect product for 200 buyers who won't pay extra is a hobby.

Second, your edge must be hard for the giant to copy. Thin fingertips alone can be copied in a season. What lasts is knowing the job better: testing in real freezers and talking to safety managers every month.

cards.title: Now it's software for vet clinics.
body: Your booking app serves veterinary clinics. A huge booking platform used by salons, gyms and doctors launches a free plan.
Clinics start asking why they should pay you. What's your move?

options.text: Launch your own free plan to stop churn
options.feedback: It may keep some users, but you're now competing on price with a company that can afford to lose money for years.

options.text: Go deeper on vets: vaccine reminders, multi-pet households, surgery prep notes
options.feedback: **Focus** and **differentiation** again. A general platform can't add pet-specific workflows without cluttering it for salons and gyms.

options.text: Expand to salons and gyms to gain scale
options.feedback: You'd step onto the giant's home ground with fewer resources, and blur what made vets choose you.

cards.title: Be much better for a few, not a bit better for all.
body: Concepts used: **Focus** (pick a narrow group) and **Differentiation** (be different in ways that group pays for). Together, they turn a big rival's size into its blind spot.
**Try it today:** name the one group your business serves best. List three things you do for them that a big rival would find awkward to copy.
